kurals.tamil:
செல்வத்துள் செல்வம் செவிச்செல்வம் அச்செல்வம்
செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Selvaththul selvam sevichchelvam achchelvam
Selvaththul ellaam thalai.
kurals.meaning: The wealth gained through the ear — the wisdom acquired by listening to the learned — is the wealth of wealth; of all kinds of wealth, it stands foremost.
kurals.elementary: People think of money, gold and houses as riches. Valluvar says the best treasure of all is what you gather by listening carefully to wise people. That kind of treasure goes into your mind, nobody can steal it, and it is worth more than any other.
kurals.university: The chapter opens with a deliberately repetitive line — செல்வம் occurs four times — which enacts its claim: among all the ‘wealths’, செவிச்செல்வம் (the wealth of the ear) is தலை, the head or chief. Placed in Porutpaal immediately after the chapters on learning (கல்வி) and its lack (கல்லாமை), this chapter supplements book-learning with கேள்வி, knowledge received orally from the learned — the dominant mode of transmitting knowledge in a largely oral culture. Parimelazhagar notes that hearing is especially valuable because it is available even to those who cannot study texts themselves, and because the ear receives the distilled result of another’s long learning. Calling it the ‘wealth’ of a treatise on polity is pointed: Valluvar ranks a cognitive possession above the material resources the rest of the book is about.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Vedas themselves are called śruti, “that which is heard”; and in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad Yajnavalkya tells Maitreyi that the Self is to be seen, to be heard (śrotavyaḥ), reflected upon and meditated upon — after she has refused his offer of worldly wealth, asking what use riches are that cannot make her immortal.
hinduism.explanation: Maitreyi turns down her husband’s property and asks instead to hear his teaching; Yajnavalkya then names hearing as the first step toward knowing the Self, and the whole Vedic canon is named after the act of hearing.
hinduism.tie_back: Maitreyi’s choice is the Kural’s ranking acted out: the wealth received through the ear is preferred over all material wealth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known dialogue; the contrast of wealth vs. hearing-as-path-to-knowledge is a very close structural match.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.”
christianity.explanation: Martha is busy serving while her sister Mary sits at Jesus’ feet listening to his word; Jesus says Mary chose the better portion, one that cannot be taken away.
christianity.tie_back: Mary’s ‘good part’ is precisely a treasure acquired by listening — like the Kural’s ear-wealth, it is the one possession that cannot be lost.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match: listening to a teacher ranked above all other occupation and as an inalienable possession.

islam.quote_or_event: “…and say, ‘My Lord, increase me in knowledge.’”
islam.explanation: The Prophet is instructed to ask God for an increase in knowledge — classical commentators note that knowledge is the only thing he is commanded to ask more of. Early Islamic knowledge was transmitted aurally (samāʿ, ‘hearing’ from a teacher).
islam.tie_back: Knowledge, not wealth, is the thing worth seeking more of — echoing the Kural’s ranking of ear-acquired knowledge above all riches.
islam._accuracy_note: Values knowledge supremely but does not specify hearing or compare it with wealth explicitly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD:”
judaism.explanation: The Shema, recited twice daily, is the central declaration of Jewish faith, and it begins with the imperative ‘Hear’. Jewish tradition treats hearing (shemaʿ, also ‘obey/understand’) as the foundational religious act.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions place hearing at the head of all things — the Shema makes listening the gateway to faith; the Kural makes it the chief of all wealth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shared primacy of hearing, but the Shema is about covenantal faith rather than ‘wealth’; the comparison is thematic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha lists seven ‘treasures’ (dhana) of a noble disciple: faith, virtue, conscience, concern for wrongdoing, learning (suta-dhana — literally ‘the treasure of what has been heard’), generosity and wisdom — declaring these superior to any worldly treasure.
buddhism.explanation: Suta means ‘heard’; a learned person in early Buddhism is bahussuta, ‘one who has heard much’. The Buddha explicitly calls this a form of wealth that cannot be taken by kings, thieves, fire or flood.
buddhism.tie_back: An almost literal parallel to செவிச்செல்வம்: hearing counted as a treasure, and ranked above material wealth.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close conceptual match — ‘treasure of hearing’ is nearly identical in wording and intent.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Agamemnon, after hearing Nestor’s counsel at Troy, wishes he had ten such counsellors among the Achaeans — then, he says, Priam’s city would soon fall.
greek_mythology.explanation: The commander of the largest Greek host values one man’s spoken advice more than numbers of soldiers or treasure.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Nestor’s counsel is wealth received through the ear; the most powerful king in the story ranks it above his other resources.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Values counsel heard over material/military resources; the ‘wealth’ framing is implicit rather than stated.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plutarch opens his essay On Listening by arguing that right listening is the beginning of right living, since the young receive virtue first through the ear, the one sense by which reason enters the soul.
philosophy.explanation: Plutarch treats hearing as the principal channel of moral formation, superior to the other senses because speech (logos) arrives through it.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Plutarch places the ear first among the means of acquiring what is truly valuable.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Moralia, De auditu (On Listening to Lectures) 1–2
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match on the primacy of hearing, though Plutarch does not use the metaphor of wealth.

kurals.tamil:
செவிக்குணவு இல்லாத போழ்து சிறிது
வயிற்றுக்கும் ஈயப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sevikkunavu illaadha pozhdhu siridhu
Vayitrrukkum eeyap padum.
kurals.meaning: Only when there is no food for the ear (no instruction to listen to) should a little be given to the stomach as well.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you are hungry but a wise teacher is speaking. Valluvar says: keep listening first! Feed your ears with good words, and only when there is nothing more to hear, give your tummy a little food.
kurals.university: The kural introduces the governing metaphor of the chapter — hearing as food (செவிக்கு உணவு) — and inverts the ordinary priority of bodily needs. The ‘உம்’ in வயிற்றுக்கும் (‘to the stomach too’) and the qualifier சிறிது (‘a little’) make the stomach a secondary and moderate claimant. Commentators read this not as a call to starve but as a hierarchy: instruction, once lost, may not recur, whereas food can be taken any time. The metaphor links this chapter to the Indian notion of the body as sustained by food and the mind by speech, and anticipates 413 (hearers as those who eat ‘ear-food’) and 420 (those who know only the mouth’s taste).

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Parikshit, cursed to die in seven days, sits by the Ganga and listens to the sage Shuka recite the Bhagavata Purana, taking neither food nor water for the entire seven days.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata frames its entire narration as a listening-fast: the king forgoes food to hear the teaching, and later says the nectar of these narrations removed his hunger and thirst.
hinduism.tie_back: A dramatic enactment of the Kural: food for the ear first, the stomach only afterward, if at all.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase; exceptionally close match to the ear-food over stomach-food priority.

christianity.quote_or_event: “It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.”
christianity.explanation: Fasting in the wilderness, Jesus rejects the tempter’s suggestion to turn stones into bread, placing the word of God above physical food.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts rank ‘the word’ as nourishment superior to bread — the Kural’s ear-food over stomach-food.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close: word as food, bodily food secondary; the Kural specifies hearing, Jesus the divine word.

islam.quote_or_event: During the Friday sermon, a trade caravan arrived and many listeners rushed out to it, leaving the Prophet standing; the Qur’an rebukes them: what is with God is better than diversion and trade, and God is the best of providers.
islam.explanation: Commentators report the caravan carried food during a time of scarcity; the verse censures those who left the sermon for provisions.
islam.tie_back: The Qur’an criticises exactly the reverse of the Kural’s order — abandoning ear-food for stomach-food.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the ‘food caravan’ detail comes from tafsir tradition rather than the verse itself.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, the days come, saith the Lord GOD, that I will send a famine in the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD:”
judaism.explanation: The prophet Amos threatens a deprivation worse than hunger: the absence of divine words to hear.
judaism.tie_back: Amos treats hearing as a form of food whose lack is a true famine — the Kural’s ‘food for the ear’ in prophetic form.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match — hearing explicitly treated as nourishment more vital than bread.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The gift of Dhamma excels all gifts; the taste of Dhamma excels all tastes; the delight in Dhamma excels all delights.”
buddhism.explanation: The verse ranks the flavour of the teaching above every other taste, including that of food.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it relocates ‘taste’ from the tongue to the teaching received — ear-food over stomach-food.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the food/taste metaphor and the ranking, but does not mention hearing specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At the Phaeacian feast, Odysseus tells King Alcinous that there is nothing more gracious than a banquet where the whole company sits listening to a bard while tables stand full of bread and meat.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Homeric ideal feast couples listening with eating — and in the Phaeacian episode the guests stay spellbound by stories deep into the night.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Homer places ear-food beside stomach-food at the feast; the Kural goes further and ranks it above.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Pairs hearing with food, but Homer treats them as complementary pleasures rather than ranking hearing first.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates warns young Hippocrates that teachings are food for the soul, and unlike food bought at market they cannot be carried home in a separate vessel and inspected first — one must take them straight into the soul by listening.
philosophy.explanation: Plato explicitly calls instruction the nourishment of the soul (psychē trephetai mathēmasi) and compares teachers to food merchants.
philosophy.tie_back: Plato and Valluvar share the metaphor of heard instruction as food, and both treat it as more consequential than bodily food.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; very close metaphor, though Plato stresses caution about what one hears rather than prioritising it over eating.

kurals.tamil:
செவியுணவின் கேள்வி உடையார் அவியுணவின்
ஆன்றாரோடு ஒப்பர் நிலத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Seviyunavin kelvi udaiyaar aviyunavin
Aandraarodu oppar nilaththu.
kurals.meaning: Those who possess learning gained by hearing — the food of the ear — are equal on earth to the gods, who feed on sacrificial oblations.
kurals.elementary: In old times people offered food to the gods through a sacred fire. Valluvar says people who ‘eat’ wise words through their ears are like gods living on earth.
kurals.university: A carefully balanced pair of compounds: செவியுணவு (ear-food) is set against அவியுணவு (oblation-food, havis), so that ‘those who have hearing’ are matched with ‘the exalted ones who eat oblations’ — the devas. Parimelazhagar glosses ஆன்றார் as the celestials; நிலத்து (‘on earth’) marks the hearers as terrestrial counterparts of the gods. The logic continues the food metaphor of 412: just as the gods are sustained by subtle offerings rather than gross food, the learned are sustained by subtle instruction. The kural thus elevates the listener’s status, not merely the value of what is heard.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna says that even one who merely listens to this teaching with faith and without envy is freed from sin and attains the auspicious worlds of the righteous.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita closes by promising elevated status — the heavenly realms of the virtuous — not only to the one who studies but to the one who simply hears it faithfully.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts raise the attentive hearer to a quasi-divine rank.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; close on status elevation of the hearer, but the Gita promises heavenly worlds rather than equality with gods on earth.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But blessed are your eyes, for they see: and your ears, for they hear. For verily I say unto you, That many prophets and righteous men have desired to see those things which ye see, and to hear those things which ye hear…”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his disciples that their hearing places them in a privileged position beyond that of prophets and the righteous of old.
christianity.tie_back: Hearing confers exalted status — the Kural likens it to divinity, Jesus to a blessedness surpassing prophets.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares ‘blessed hearers’ theme; lacks the food/oblation imagery and equality with gods.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said that no people gather in a house of God reciting and studying the Book among themselves but that tranquillity descends on them, mercy covers them, the angels surround them, and God mentions them among those who are with Him.
islam.explanation: Those who gather to hear and study revelation are placed in the company of angels and in God’s own presence.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s hearers ‘equal to the gods’, these listeners are drawn into the celestial company while still on earth.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known hadith; close on celestial company for listeners/learners.

judaism.quote_or_event: When Israel at Sinai said “we will do and we will hear” (naʿaseh ve-nishma), the Talmud relates that a heavenly voice asked, “Who revealed to My children this secret that the ministering angels use?” — and angels crowned each Israelite.
judaism.explanation: By committing themselves to hearing, the people adopted the manner of angels and were honoured as such.
judaism.tie_back: An almost exact parallel: devoted hearers are made equal to celestial beings on earth.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of aggadic passage; strong structural match (hearers likened to angels).

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Mangala Sutta lists among the ‘highest blessings’ much learning (bahusacca — literally ‘much hearing’) and hearing the Dhamma at the proper time (kālena dhammassavanaṃ); the discourse is spoken in reply to a deva, and its close says those who fulfil these blessings are everywhere victorious and go everywhere in safety.
buddhism.explanation: Hearing is counted among the supreme blessings discussed between the Buddha and the gods.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural exalts the hearer to divine rank; the Mangala Sutta, addressed to gods, counts hearing among the highest blessings.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Honours hearing highly but does not equate hearers with gods; best available Buddhist parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod describes the Muses singing on Olympus and delighting the great mind of Zeus with their song — the gods, who feast on nectar and ambrosia, also feast on what they hear.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth, listening to song is itself one of the divine pleasures on Olympus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both imagine the gods as consumers of a subtle ‘food’; the Kural makes human listeners share that divine diet.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak-to-moderate: gods delight in hearing, but no claim that human listeners equal gods.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pythagoras’ school admitted novices as akousmatikoi, ‘listeners’, who spent years in silence hearing the master’s sayings; the tradition held Pythagoras himself to be a divine or semi-divine figure whose hearers participated in his wisdom.
philosophy.explanation: Listening was the defining activity of the first rank of Pythagorean disciples, and the community treated the teaching as quasi-divine.
philosophy.tie_back: The Pythagorean ‘hearers’ are an institutional version of the Kural’s honoured listeners, drawing near to the divine through the ear.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Historical parallel on institutionalised listening; the ‘equal to gods’ element is only indirect.

kurals.tamil:
கற்றிலன் ஆயினும் கேட்க அஃதொருவற்கு
ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்றாந் துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Katrilan aayinum ketka aqdhoruvarku
Orkaththin ootraandh thunai.
kurals.meaning: Even if a person has not studied, let him listen to the learned; that hearing will be a supporting staff to him in times of weakness and adversity.
kurals.elementary: Maybe you never got to go to school or read many books. That’s okay — just listen to wise people! What you hear will be like a walking stick that holds you up when life gets hard.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar extends the chapter’s value to the unlettered: கற்றிலன் ஆயினும் (‘though he has not learned’) concedes lack of formal study, but கேட்க is an imperative — listening remains possible for everyone. ஒற்கம் means weakness, falling, or distress; ஊற்று is a prop or support (the same word recurs in 415 as ஊற்றுக்கோல், ‘supporting staff’). The kural thus democratises knowledge in an oral society: hearing is a route to wisdom for those without access to texts, and its value is practical — it sustains one when fortune slips.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna says there are others who, not knowing the paths of knowledge themselves, hear the teaching from others and worship accordingly; by devotion to what they have heard, they too cross beyond death.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita explicitly accommodates the untrained seeker who relies only on hearing from the wise, and promises that such hearing carries him through.
hinduism.tie_back: Close match: the unlearned who listens is supported and saved by what he hears.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; nearly the same argument as the Kural — hearing substitutes for learning and supports in the gravest distress.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: On trial before the council, two fishermen without formal schooling speak with confidence; their strength came from having heard Jesus.
christianity.tie_back: Unlearned yet sustained in adversity by what they had heard — a vivid enactment of the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on both elements: lack of study and support in a crisis through hearing.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet prayed for God to brighten the face of one who hears a saying, memorises it and conveys it — for many a carrier of knowledge is not himself learned, and many carry it to one who understands it better.
islam.explanation: The hadith honours the listener-transmitter even if he is not a scholar, recognising hearing as a path to knowledge open to all.
islam.tie_back: Both texts affirm that the unlearned can still become possessors of knowledge through hearing.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches the unlearned-hearer theme but not the ‘support in adversity’ element.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then Samuel answered, Speak; for thy servant heareth.”
judaism.explanation: The boy Samuel, of whom the text says he ‘did not yet know the LORD’ (3:7), is taught by Eli simply to listen; his hearing makes him a prophet who later sustains Israel in crisis.
judaism.tie_back: Lack of learning is no barrier: Samuel begins with nothing but a listening ear, which becomes his lifelong support.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on unlearned listener; ‘support in adversity’ is implicit in Samuel’s later role.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Paṭācārā, having lost her husband, children, parents and brother in quick succession, wanders half-mad with grief; on hearing the Buddha’s words she regains her mind and later becomes an arahant and teacher.
buddhism.explanation: The commentary on the Dhammapada tells how a woman with no learning, in the depth of misfortune, was restored by listening to the Buddha.
buddhism.tie_back: Hearing as ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்று — the prop that held her up when she had fallen.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Narrative paraphrase from the commentarial tradition; strong fit on support in distress.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Lost and unable to find his way home, Odysseus is sent by Circe to the underworld to hear the prophet Tiresias, whose words guide him through the dangers that follow.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, for all his cunning, lacks the knowledge he needs; he must go and listen to one who knows.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hearing the wise supplies what one’s own learning lacks, and supports one through adversity.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate: the hearing-as-support element fits; Odysseus is not ‘unlearned’ in the Kural’s sense.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the myth of Theuth, King Thamus warns that writing will give pupils the appearance of wisdom without its reality, since they will have ‘heard many things without instruction’; Socrates argues that living speech exchanged with a knowledgeable teacher is superior to written texts.
philosophy.explanation: Plato privileges oral teaching over book-learning as the true vehicle of understanding.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar likewise reassures the one without book-learning that listening to the learned is itself a reliable path to wisdom.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match on oral over written learning; the ‘support in adversity’ element is absent.

kurals.tamil:
இழுக்கல் உடையுழி ஊற்றுக்கோல் அற்றே
ஒழுக்கம் உடையார்வாய்ச் சொல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Izhukkal udaiyuzhi ootrukkol atre
Ozhukkam udaiyaarvaaich chol.
kurals.meaning: The words from the mouths of the virtuous are like a supporting staff to one walking on slippery ground.
kurals.elementary: When you walk on a muddy, slippery path, a strong stick helps you not fall. Advice from good, honest people works the same way — it keeps you steady when life gets slippery.
kurals.university: The image is precise: இழுக்கல் is slipperiness (and by extension moral lapse), ஊற்றுக்கோல் a staff one leans on. The kural qualifies the source of hearing — not any speaker, but ஒழுக்கம் உடையார், those of upright conduct. Parimelazhagar emphasises that the words of the virtuous are trustworthy because their conduct confirms them, and that such words prevent a fall before it happens. The kural links the chapter to the earlier chapter on ஒழுக்கமுடைமை (conduct) and grounds the authority of what one hears in the moral character of the speaker.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Arise, awake; approach the great and learn. The path is sharp as a razor’s edge, difficult to cross, hard to tread — so say the wise.”
hinduism.explanation: The Katha Upanishad describes the spiritual path as treacherous and tells the seeker to approach and hear the great teachers.
hinduism.tie_back: A hazardous path and the counsel of the wise as one’s support — the same structure as the Kural’s slippery ground and staff.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Standard rendering paraphrased (translations vary); close image of dangerous path plus guidance of the wise.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:”
christianity.explanation: The one who hears and acts on Jesus’ words stands firm when rain, floods and winds come.
christianity.tie_back: Heard words from a righteous teacher as the stable footing against collapse — the Kural’s staff on slippery ground.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on stability through heard words; image is foundation rather than staff.

islam.quote_or_event: “And hold firmly to the rope of Allah all together and do not become divided.”
islam.explanation: Commentators interpret the ‘rope of Allah’ as the Qur’an and the guidance transmitted through it — something to grip to avoid falling.
islam.tie_back: A physical support image (rope / staff) for guidance received from a trustworthy source.
islam._accuracy_note: Similar support metaphor; the source is revelation rather than virtuous human speakers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The law of his God is in his heart; none of his steps shall slide.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist says the one who has taken God’s teaching into his heart will not slip.
judaism.tie_back: Teaching received and held keeps one’s steps from sliding — near-identical imagery to the Kural’s slippery ground.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close image (not slipping); the Psalm’s source is divine law rather than the speech of the virtuous.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure. It is always better, and never worse, to cultivate such an association.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha urges following the corrective words of the wise, who save one from error.
buddhism.tie_back: Words of the wise as a guide that prevents a fall — the Kural’s supporting staff.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close on the value of heeding the virtuous; image differs (guide to treasure vs staff).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: As Odysseus walks toward Circe’s house, Hermes meets him, warns him of her drugs and gives him the herb moly with instructions; heeding this counsel, Odysseus avoids being turned into a swine like his men.
greek_mythology.explanation: A trustworthy divine adviser’s words save the hero at the moment of greatest danger.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Counsel heard at the right moment keeps one from ‘slipping’ into ruin.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate: shared idea of timely advice preventing a fall; Hermes is a god rather than a ‘virtuous person’.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca advises Lucilius to choose some man of high character and keep him always before his eyes, living as if he were watching — ‘we need someone against whom our characters can measure themselves’.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca argues that most wrongdoing is prevented when a witness of good character stands near the one about to err.
philosophy.tie_back: The upright person serves as the support that keeps one from slipping — Valluvar’s staff.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; stresses the example rather than the speech of the virtuous, but the protective function matches.

kurals.tamil:
எனைத்தானும் நல்லவை கேட்க அனைத்தானும்
ஆன்ற பெருமை தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Enaiththaanum nallavai ketka anaiththaanum
Aandra perumai tharum.
kurals.meaning: Let one listen to good things, however little; even that little will bring full greatness.
kurals.elementary: You don’t have to listen to a huge lecture. Even hearing one small good idea is worth it, because even a little bit of goodness can make you a much better person.
kurals.university: The kural balances எனைத்தானும் (‘however little’) against அனைத்தானும் (‘to that very extent’), so that the benefit is proportionate to what is heard, yet always leads to ஆன்ற பெருமை — full, well-rounded greatness. Two conditions are embedded: the content must be நல்லவை (good things), and the act must be real listening. The couplet thus both encourages even small, occasional listening and implicitly warns against hearing what is not good — a selectivity that parallels many traditions’ counsel about what one lets into the ear.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Shanti mantra “bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ śṛṇuyāma devāḥ” — “O gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; may we see with our eyes what is auspicious.”
hinduism.explanation: Recited at the opening of the Mundaka and Prashna Upanishads, this Rig Vedic prayer asks that the ear receive only what is good.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts direct the ear specifically toward ‘good things’ (நல்லவை / bhadram).
hinduism.source: Rig Veda 1.89.8; peace invocation of the Mundaka and Prashna Upanishads
hinduism._accuracy_note: Translations vary, so marked as paraphrase; very close match on hearing good things.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Take heed what ye hear: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns his hearers to be careful what they listen to, and promises increase to those who hear rightly.
christianity.tie_back: Selective hearing of what is good leads to growth — the Kural’s ‘however little, it brings greatness’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on both selectivity and proportional reward for hearing.

islam.quote_or_event: “Who listen to speech and follow the best of it. Those are the ones Allah has guided, and those are people of understanding.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who listen discerningly and adopt the best of what they hear.
islam.tie_back: Both texts value hearing selectively for the good, and connect it with honour/understanding.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; lacks the ‘however little’ emphasis.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Zoma asks, “Who is wise?” and answers, “One who learns from every person,” citing the Psalm: “From all my teachers I have gained understanding.”
judaism.explanation: Wisdom comes from gathering good teaching from every source, however humble.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it urges taking in good wherever and in whatever measure it is found.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; close on gathering good from all quarters; less explicit about hearing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Better than a thousand useless words is one useful word, hearing which one attains peace.”
buddhism.explanation: A single beneficial word heard is worth more than any quantity of empty speech.
buddhism.tie_back: Near-identical point: even a small amount of good hearing yields great benefit.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close — explicitly about hearing a little that is good.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe, Odysseus stops his crew’s ears with wax so they cannot hear the Sirens, whose beautiful song lures sailors to death; only he listens, bound to the mast.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Sirens are the classic Greek warning that not everything pleasant to hear is good.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The negative counterpart of the Kural: hear what is good (நல்லவை), and guard the ear against what destroys.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Inverse illustration — about what not to hear rather than the value of a little good hearing.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca advises Lucilius to acquire each day something that will fortify him against poverty, death and other misfortunes, and to select one thought daily to digest thoroughly.
philosophy.explanation: Small daily portions of good teaching, well absorbed, build lasting strength of character.
philosophy.tie_back: Even a little good taken in regularly yields greatness — the Kural’s ‘however little’.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; concerns reading as well as hearing, but the ‘small portion, large benefit’ logic matches.

kurals.tamil:
பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் பேதைமை சொல்லார் இழைத்துணர்ந்து
ஈண்டிய கேள்வி யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Pizhaiththunarndhum pedhaimai sollaar izhaiththunarndhu
Eendiya kelvi yavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who have examined things minutely and gathered abundant learning by hearing will not speak foolishly, even when they have misunderstood something.
kurals.elementary: Everyone makes mistakes sometimes. But a person who has listened carefully to lots of wise people won’t say silly things even when they get confused, because all that good listening keeps them careful.
kurals.university: The paired participles பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் (‘even having understood wrongly’) and இழைத்துணர்ந்து (‘having understood finely, as if threading’) frame the couplet. இழை (thread) suggests minute, careful examination; ஈண்டிய (‘amassed’) describes accumulated hearing. The kural is realistic: the learned may still err in perception, but their trained habit of mind prevents error from becoming foolish speech (பேதைமை). Hearing thus functions as a safeguard not of infallibility but of judgment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna to learn the truth by approaching the wise, through reverent submission, thorough questioning (paripraśnena) and service; the knowers of truth will instruct him.
hinduism.explanation: Pariprashna — questioning repeatedly and thoroughly — is the Gita’s equivalent of இழைத்துணர்தல், careful probing examination of what is heard.
hinduism.tie_back: Knowledge carefully examined through hearing and questioning produces sound judgment and speech.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches the method (careful hearing and inquiry) but not the claim about not speaking foolishly when mistaken.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good… for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: What one has stored within shapes what one says.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘amassed hearing’ is such a treasure — it ensures that even in error the speech is not foolish.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on stored inner resources shaping speech; lacks the ‘even when mistaken’ nuance.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet said: whoever believes in God and the Last Day should speak what is good or keep silent.
islam.explanation: Restraint in speech — speaking only good or not at all — is framed as a mark of faith.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s learned hearers, the believer avoids foolish speech even when uncertain, by choosing silence.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; concerns guarding speech but not the role of accumulated hearing.

judaism.quote_or_event: Among the seven traits of the wise: he does not interrupt, is not hasty to answer, asks and answers to the point, and about what he has not heard he says, “I have not heard.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah’s portrait of the sage emphasises careful listening and restraint in speaking where knowledge is lacking.
judaism.tie_back: The well-heard sage avoids foolish speech — precisely the Kural’s claim about those of amassed hearing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match on the disciplined speech of those trained in hearing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares one who learns the teaching without examining its meaning to a man grasping a water-snake by the tail and being bitten, while one who examines the meaning with wisdom grasps it correctly, like seizing a snake with a forked stick.
buddhism.explanation: Mere hearing is dangerous; hearing coupled with careful examination yields right understanding and right use.
buddhism.tie_back: Corresponds to the Kural’s இழைத்துணர்ந்து — finely examined hearing that prevents foolish error.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches ‘careful examination of what is heard’, less the claim about speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Nestor, the aged king of Pylos, ‘from whose tongue speech flowed sweeter than honey’, rises to calm the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles, drawing on the counsel of the great men he has heard and lived among.
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor’s long experience of listening to heroes of earlier generations makes his speech measured and wise.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Amassed hearing yields speech free of folly, even amid a crisis.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate; Nestor exemplifies wise speech from long experience, though his advice here is ignored.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle says we ought to attend to the undemonstrated sayings and opinions of experienced and older people, or of people of practical wisdom, no less than to demonstrations, because experience has given them an eye to see aright.
philosophy.explanation: Practical wisdom accumulated through experience produces sound judgment even without formal proof.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it credits accumulated, well-examined learning with reliable judgment and speech.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase (standard Ross wording closely followed); concerns experience broadly rather than hearing specifically.

kurals.tamil:
கேட்பினும் கேளாத் தகையவே கேள்வியால்
தோட்கப் படாத செவி.
kurals.transliteration:
Ketpinum kelaath thagaiyave kelviyaal
Thotkap padaadha sevi.
kurals.meaning: Ears that have not been pierced by instruction, though they hear sounds, are no better than deaf.
kurals.elementary: Your ears can hear noises all day, but if you never really listen to wise lessons, it’s almost like your ears don’t work. Real hearing means letting good lessons get inside.
kurals.university: The pun turns on கேள் (‘hear’): ears may கேட்பினும் (hear sounds) yet be கேளாத் தகைய (of the nature of not hearing, i.e., deaf) if not தோட்கப்பட்ட — ‘bored, pierced’ — by கேள்வி. The piercing alludes to the ear-boring ritual (and earrings) of Tamil custom: the true ornament and opening of the ear is instruction. The distinction between physiological hearing and receptive understanding is the heart of the kural and finds close echoes in prophetic and philosophical literature on ‘hearing without hearing’.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Katha Upanishad says of the Self: many do not even get to hear of it, and many, even hearing of it, do not comprehend it; wonderful is the teacher and wonderful the one who learns it.
hinduism.explanation: Mere hearing is not enough — receptive understanding is rare.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘ears that hear yet are deaf’ in Upanishadic form.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore speak I to them in parables: because they seeing see not; and hearing they hear not, neither do they understand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus distinguishes physical hearing from receptive understanding.
christianity.tie_back: Almost verbatim the Kural’s paradox: hearing, yet not hearing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on the core paradox.

islam.quote_or_event: “Deaf, dumb and blind — so they will not return [to the right path].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes those who reject guidance as deaf though their physical hearing is intact.
islam.tie_back: Ears untouched by guidance are counted as deaf — as in the Kural.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on functional deafness of unreceptive ears.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear now this, O foolish people, and without understanding; which have eyes, and see not; which have ears, and hear not:”
judaism.explanation: Jeremiah rebukes a people whose senses function but whose understanding is closed.
judaism.tie_back: Same paradox as the Kural: working ears, no real hearing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though all his life a fool associates with a wise man, he no more comprehends the Truth than a spoon tastes the flavor of the soup.”
buddhism.explanation: Proximity to teaching does not guarantee reception; the fool is like a spoon that touches soup without tasting it.
buddhism.tie_back: The fool’s ears, like the spoon, contact wisdom without taking it in — the Kural’s ‘unpierced ear’.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on exposure without reception.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Cassandra, cursed by Apollo, prophesies truly the fall of Troy and Agamemnon’s murder, but those who hear her words do not take them in; in Aeschylus the chorus hears her plainly yet cannot understand.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Trojans and later the Argive elders hear the truth but remain effectively deaf to it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A mythic image of ears that hear yet do not hear.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good illustration, though the failure is caused by a curse rather than lack of instruction.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Heraclitus: those who do not understand, even when they have heard, are like the deaf; the saying bears witness of them — ‘present, they are absent’.
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus distinguishes hearing the logos from understanding it; the unreceptive are functionally deaf.
philosophy.tie_back: Nearly identical to the Kural: hearing without instruction is deafness.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the fragment (translations vary); a near one-to-one match.

kurals.tamil:
நுணங்கிய கேள்வியர் அல்லார் வணங்கிய
வாயினர் ஆதல் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Nunangiya kelviyar allaar vanangiya
Vaayinar aadhal aridhu.
kurals.meaning: It is hard for those who lack subtle, refined learning gained by hearing to possess humble, courteous speech.
kurals.elementary: People who have listened a lot to wise teachers usually speak kindly and humbly. People who haven’t listened much often find it hard to speak gently and politely.
kurals.university: Two adjectives govern the couplet: நுணங்கிய (fine, subtle) describes the quality of hearing, and வணங்கிய (bowed, humble) the quality of speech. The link is causal: refined hearing produces humility in speech, because the listener becomes aware of how much others know. Parimelazhagar reads வணங்கிய வாய் as speech that is modest and respectful. The kural thus connects the ear and the mouth: good speaking is an outcome of good listening — a theme echoed widely in wisdom literature that advises being quick to hear and slow to speak.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Gita defines austerity of speech as words that cause no distress, that are truthful, pleasant and beneficial, together with regular study and recitation of the scriptures (svādhyāya).
hinduism.explanation: Gentle, truthful speech is paired with regular learning of the sacred texts.
hinduism.tie_back: Both link cultivated learning with courteous, humble speech.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; pairs learning with gentle speech but does not state the causal claim explicitly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:”
christianity.explanation: James makes hearing the precondition of restrained, gentle speech.
christianity.tie_back: Listening first produces humble speech — the Kural’s causal link between hearing and mouth.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on hearing preceding restrained speech.

islam.quote_or_event: “And be moderate in your pace and lower your voice; indeed, the most disagreeable of sounds is the voice of donkeys.”
islam.explanation: Part of the counsel of Luqman the Wise to his son; wisdom expresses itself as humble, lowered speech.
islam.tie_back: Wisdom received through a sage’s counsel issues in humble speech.
islam._accuracy_note: Matches humble speech arising from wise instruction; the ‘refined hearing’ element is implicit.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools… let thy words be few.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes counsels readiness to hear and restraint of speech as marks of wisdom.
judaism.tie_back: Hearing first, then few and humble words — close to the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on hearing and restrained speech.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Dhammapada praises the monk who controls his tongue, speaks in moderation, is unassuming and explains the teaching in letter and spirit — his speech is pleasing.
buddhism.explanation: Mastery of the teaching produces restrained, modest and sweet speech.
buddhism.tie_back: Refined learning yielding humble speech — as in the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; close on learned humility in speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Young Telemachus, sent by Athena to question Nestor, protests that he is inexperienced in subtle speech and that it is shameful for a young man to question an elder; Athena encourages him, and he addresses Nestor with deference.
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus’ speech is modest precisely because he knows he has come to listen and learn.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The posture of a hearer produces respectful, humble speech.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Moderate illustration; not a direct statement of the principle.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Zeno of Citium, rebuking a talkative youth, said that we have two ears and one mouth so that we may listen more and speak less.
philosophy.explanation: The Stoic founder makes the proportion of hearing to speaking a matter of wisdom.
philosophy.tie_back: Listening more produces measured, humble speech — the Kural’s link.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 7.23
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely cited anecdote; close in spirit.

kurals.tamil:
செவியிற் சுவையுணரா வாயுணர்வின் மாக்கள்
அவியினும் வாழினும் என்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seviyir suvaiyunaraa vaayunarvin maakkal
Aviyinum vaazhinum en.
kurals.meaning: What does it matter whether they die or live — those beast-like people who know only the tastes of the mouth and not the tastes of the ear?
kurals.elementary: Some people only care about yummy food and never enjoy listening to wise words. Valluvar says, sharply, that such people live like animals — whether they live or die makes little difference to the world.
kurals.university: The closing kural returns to the food metaphor of 412–413 with a stinging contrast between செவியிற் சுவை (the ear’s taste) and வாயுணர்வு (mouth-knowledge, i.e., the palate). மாக்கள் denotes people without discernment — often glossed as ‘beast-like men’. The rhetorical question அவியினும் வாழினும் என் (‘whether they perish or live, what of it?’) declares their existence inconsequential. Some commentators take வாயுணர்வு as knowing only what one’s own mouth says, i.e., talkers who never listen; either way the chapter closes by denying full humanity to those who never cultivate hearing.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Eating, sleeping, fear and mating are common to humans and animals; dharma alone is the distinguishing feature of humans, and without it they are equal to beasts.
hinduism.explanation: A famous verse in the introduction to the Hitopadesha defines human distinctiveness by something beyond the appetites.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s judgment: those who know only the appetites are மாக்கள், beast-like.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known subhashita; strong match, though it names dharma rather than hearing.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul condemns those governed by appetite and earthly concerns.
christianity.tie_back: Those who know only the mouth’s taste — ‘whose God is their belly’ — are judged as worthless as the Kural’s மாக்கள்.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on appetite-driven life; lacks the ear/hearing contrast.

islam.quote_or_event: “…They have hearts with which they do not understand, they have eyes with which they do not see, and they have ears with which they do not hear. Those are like livestock; rather, they are more astray.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an compares those with unused ears to cattle — even lower.
islam.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural: those without the ‘taste of the ear’ are beast-like.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: unhearing ears and comparison with animals.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Man that is in honour, and understandeth not, is like the beasts that perish.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist says a person without understanding, however prosperous, is no better than an animal.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts equate a life without understanding with that of beasts.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the beast comparison; hearing is not mentioned explicitly.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The man of little learning grows old like a bull. He grows only in bulk, but his wisdom does not grow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Pali appassuta — ‘one who has heard little’ — is compared to an ox that merely grows fat.
buddhism.tie_back: The one who has not heard lives like a beast — precisely the Kural’s மாக்கள்.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: the ‘little-heard’ person likened to an animal living only for the body.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When King Midas judged Pan’s rustic piping superior to Apollo’s lyre, Apollo would not let such dull ears keep human shape and gave him the ears of an ass.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s myth punishes an ear without taste by making it literally bestial; Midas had earlier shown the same folly in preferring gold, which turned even his food to metal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ears that do not ‘taste’ properly mark a person as beast-like — the Kural’s மாக்கள் image in myth.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong imagery match (tasteless ears made bestial); the context is music rather than wisdom.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato says those without wisdom and virtue, always occupied with feasting, look downward like cattle, bent over their tables, feeding and fattening and breeding.
philosophy.explanation: The lover of bodily pleasure lives like grazing cattle, never tasting true pleasure.
philosophy.tie_back: A life devoted to the mouth rather than the mind is bestial — the Kural’s verdict.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong match on appetite-bound life as bestial.
